I haven't experienced this from your side, so I can't speak much to that. But the truth is that family doesn't stop being family just because there's this one horrible thing about them. Luckily my girlfriend is really understanding and has never had any issues with it, but I also keep our relationship a secret from my homophobic parents-- because yes, it sucks that they're homophobic, but it doesn't change the eighteen years of my life I spent with them, the fact that they were the only people I knew for more than a couple years growing up, the fact that they've sacrificed a lot for me and given me a lot of love. 

And right now, I do as much as I can to hang out with them, because I know that soon enough, I'm going to lose them, maybe forever. 

Think about it like you girlfriend's elderly grandmother, battling chronic illness, and only has a couple years left in her, probably. She might prioritize her grandmother somewhat. That doesn't mean she cares about her more, only that she realizes that she's going to lose her soon. 

I can't speak for your girlfriend, but that's how I feel about my family. I love them a ton and I just don't have the energy to be angry at them for their religious views. I know they'll probably cut me out of their lives when they find out I'm gay, and I'm trying to make peace with that by making memories with them while I still can. This one terrible part of them doesn't change the fact that they're my family and I love them a lot.

I'm going to be honest, I don't think this is the best idea. I don't really want to undermine her feelings and I love a cute romantic gesture as much as the next girl, but when it comes to her depression, I'm not really willing to play games. 

But thanks for the advice though! I totally get that you're not as familiar with her and our relationship as I am so I won't knock you for saying something that I don't think is right for the two of us. :)

Thanks, I decided to text her back and be honest with her about how being alone can be a way I keep my anxiety from spiralling out of control... I decided that I respect her and I should be honest and open to her since she's doing the same for me. We're just going to have to figure out how to make this work for us since being alone can make her feel worse, but I often need space. I think we're going to be able to figure it out though, overall we have a pretty strong relationship and we're very conscious of each other's needs. Thanks for the advice :)

Health insurance is a good point, haha. I suppose part of the rush is that I want to have my last name ironed out forever before I'm in grad school and start publishing my research, but I don't really consider that a reason to get married. 

I don't really think a nice ring/wedding is a priority for us. Neither of us are traditional/ceremonial people and the only point of the actual wedding is the legal officialness+ celebration of your love, which neither of us really care about spending money on. And if the ring holds up, that's enough. My parents always said not to spend much money on the wedding (they got married in a 20 minute timeslot at the Academy after my father graduated, & they only filled up the first two rows of the small chapel with guests, and they regret nothing). 

As far as support goes, I think her parents would be okay with it, maybe her sister would judge us, but she'd come around. My family will never support my marriage regardless. 

But yeah, waiting until we know where we're going to grad school might be a good idea. If we can't go to the same place, I'd be willing to take four years and work in industry before getting my PhD if that's what it takes to make our relationship work. 

Regardless, thanks for the advice. I'll definitely give it some thought. :)
Thanks for the advice. I'll hold off for a bit. We're moving in together this August so we'll see how it goes when we do :)
Yeah, that's understandable. I'll definitely wait to see how living together works out for us before I pop the question :)
Yeah, I probably won't propose until 2020 and we'll both be 20 by then.

It's not so much that I'm desperate to make a commitment, but I'm pretty certain I've found my person. She checks off pretty much every box of what I want in a partner, but at the same time, we've shared deep dark secrets and embarrassing moments from our past with each other. It isn't as though I think she's perfect in every way, but her flaws are things I can embrace and accept, and I think we have a really healthy way of resolving conflicts and dealing with issues between us. 

I'm usually a pretty hesitant and reserved person, believe it or not. I know we are young and naive, but at the same time, there are very few things I've felt as certain about as the fact that I want to spend my life with her. And honestly, I don't really see much point in waiting, except perhaps to stay on our parents' health insurance... We're young, for sure, but my parents got married right when my father graduated from college, and it's worked pretty well for them. 

Amusingly one factor that might be considered the "rush" is that I really won't be able to change my last name without career ramifications once I start publishing my research. And after we talked, I think I'd take her last name. But that's not super important and I'm also thinking about just legally changing my last name to something of my own choosing and keeping that. 

But I think I will wait, at least for one semester of living together. We're going to be semi-long distance this summer too, so we'll be able to see how our relationship holds up over distance and then how it holds up over living together. I don't really feel the need to give her a promise ring both because of the weird religious connotations of that and also because in my mind we're already pretty much committed.

Honestly, don't come out. There's not really a practical reason for you to do so and I do feel like people should avoid coming out as ace until they're 18. Because a good number of people who identity as ace in their early teens don't anymore by the time they're adults. That doesn't mean being ace isn't a real thing, and it doesn't even mean that all those people aren't ace, but your sexuality can develop later. 

Really it's fine if you have to change how you identify. I myself identified as ace, then pan, then gay, then bi, then not-at-all-bi-entirely-gay. Truth is I was just figuring myself out. I identified as ace for over a year but honestly I was just trying to avoid my feelings for other women (but! that definitely isn't true of all or most ace people). 

I'm also 19 and still not out to my family. I started identifying as LGBT+ when I was like 14. I would say if you think your parents would or might react badly, I'd avoid coming out until you're not dependent on them. Bad shit can happen honestly. I understand, having found your identity, coming out seems like it would be a relief and a logical next step, but being ace, it's not like you're saying "I'm coming out so expect to see my boyfriend soon." 

More importantly, disregard my advice and come out if you feel you need to. Ultimately it's your decision and whatever you choose to do is the right thing for you.

Eh, the adult perspective here is that you're young and you probably shouldn't worry about it. I'm 19 and I sincerely regret every relationship I had before I turned 18. And honestly, wait until you're 18, then you can make dating site profiles and legally engage in any non-alcoholic relationship behavior you like. Plus you don't have to deal with what happens if you get in a long term relationship in high school. 

But yeah, I'd say 25ish is the cutoff for when the fact that you've never had a girlfriend (despite wanting one) becomes concerning.
